title: Pointers, part 1
goal: Understand addresses and pointer variables, read and write through a pointer with *, use NULL safely, and write functions like swap that change the caller's variables through pointer parameters.

topics.title: Addresses, & and pointer variables
topics.examNote: Exam traces (2016F Q3) start with `int *p, *q, *r;` and lines like `p = &a;`. You must know what `&a` gives and what a pointer variable holds, and be able to draw it.

blocks.text:
### Memory is a row of numbered boxes

Your program's memory is a long row of **bytes**. Each byte has a number called its **address**, like a house number on a street.

Every variable you declare is an **object**: a piece of memory that holds a value. An `int` uses 4 bytes and a `double` uses 8. The **address of an object** is the address of its first byte.

We draw memory as a table. The addresses below are *pretend* addresses chosen to be easy to read. Real ones are long hexadecimal numbers like `0x7ffd6d831cac`.

```c
int a = 99;
int b = 55;
```

| address | name | value |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | `a` | 99 |
| 1004 | `b` | 55 |

`a` starts at 1000 and fills bytes 1000 to 1003, so `b` can start at 1004.

### `&` gives an address; a pointer stores one

The **address-of operator** `&` gives you the address of an object. With the table above, `&a` is 1000 and `&b` is 1004.

A **pointer** is a value that is an address. A **pointer variable** is a variable that stores a pointer. The notebook says: if `T` is a type, then `T *` is the type of a pointer that can store the address of a `T` object.

```c
int a = 99;
int *ptr = &a;     // ptr gets the address of a
```

Read `int *ptr` as "`ptr` is a **pointer to int**". It can hold the address of any `int`.

| address | name | value |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | `a` | 99 |
| 1008 | `ptr` | 1000 |

The pointer is an object too. It has its own address (1008) and its own value (1000, the address of `a`). On our 64-bit machines every pointer takes 8 bytes. We also draw it with an arrow: "`ptr` **points to** `a`".

```
    ptr                 a
  +------+          +------+
  | 1000 | -------> |  99  |
  +------+          +------+
   @1008             @1000
```

blocks.q: Why does a pointer have a type (`int *`, `double *`) and not just "address"?
blocks.a: An address only says where an object *starts*. The type says how many bytes the object uses and how to read them: 4 bytes as an `int`, or 8 bytes as a `double`. Tomorrow's arithmetic on pointers also needs the size.

blocks.text:
### Pointing somewhere else

A pointer variable can be changed like any variable. Giving it a new address makes it point at a different object. The objects themselves do not change.

```c
int a = 99;
int *ptr = &a;   // ptr points at a

int b = 55;
ptr = &b;        // now ptr points at b; a is still 99
```

The types must match: `ptr` is an `int *`, so it should only get addresses of `int` objects. For a `double d`, you need a `double *`: `double *dp = &d;`.

The `*` belongs to **one** name. `int *p, q;` makes `p` an `int *` but `q` a plain `int`. To declare three pointers on one line write `int *p, *q, *r;` (as in the 2016 final). gcc catches the mistake when you store an address in `q`:

blocks.caption: twodecl.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o twodecl twodecl.c
twodecl.c: In function 'main':
twodecl.c:7:7: warning: assignment to 'int' from 'int *' makes integer from pointer without a cast [-Wint-conversion]
    7 |     q = &a;
      |       ^
blocks.caption: A warning means the program is almost certainly wrong. Fix it with int *p, *q; (and make q print *q).

blocks.text:
### Printing an address with `%p`

`printf` prints a pointer with the conversion `%p`. `%p` expects the general pointer type `void *` (Day 12 explains it), so the habit is to **cast** the pointer: `(void *) ptr`. The output is the address in hexadecimal (base 16, starting `0x`).

This program also uses `*ptr`, which you learn in the next lesson: it means "the `int` that `ptr` points to".

blocks.caption: addr.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o addr addr.c
$ ./addr
a           = 99
&a          = 0x7ffd6d831cac
ptr         = 0x7ffd6d831cac
*ptr        = 99
&ptr        = 0x7ffd6d831cb0
sizeof(ptr) = 8
$ ./addr
a           = 99
&a          = 0x7ffd326785dc
ptr         = 0x7ffd326785dc
*ptr        = 99
&ptr        = 0x7ffd326785e0
sizeof(ptr) = 8
blocks.caption: Two runs. The addresses are different every time (Linux places memory at a random spot on each run, for security), so yours will differ too. What never changes: ptr always equals &a, and the pointer is 8 bytes.

blocks.text: Type in addr.c, compile it with gcc -std=c17 -Wall and run it three times. Check that the &a and ptr lines always match each other, even though they change from run to run. Then add a double d = 2.5; and a double *dp = &d; and print both with %p.

blocks.q: Pretend addresses: `double d = 2.5;` is at 2000 and `double *dp = &d;` is at 2008. What are the type and value of `&d`? What is the value of `dp`? What is `&dp`?
blocks.a: `&d` has type `double *` and value 2000. `dp` holds 2000 (it points at `d`). `&dp` is 2008, the address of the pointer variable itself.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Every object (variable) lives at an **address**; `&x` gives the address of `x`.
- `T *p` declares `p` as a **pointer to T**: a variable that holds the address of a `T` object. It is an object too, with its own address (8 bytes on our machines).
- Draw memory as a table (address, name, value) or as boxes with arrows.
- A pointer can be changed to point at another object: `p = &b;`.
- `int *p, q;` makes only `p` a pointer. Write `int *p, *q;`.
- Print addresses with `%p` and `(void *) p`; the values change from run to run.

topics.title: Dereferencing with *, and NULL
topics.examNote: 2016F Q3 (10 marks) was a pure trace: three `int`s, three pointers, assignments like `p = q;`, `*p = *q;`, `*r = *q + 1;`, and printf lines to predict. Draw the memory table and update it line by line. The quiz has two traces in the same style.

blocks.text:
### `*` follows the pointer

The notebook quotes Wikipedia: a pointer is like a page number in a book's index. **Dereferencing** the pointer means turning to that page and reading what is there.

In C the **dereference operator** is `*` written in front of a pointer. If `ptr` points at `a`, then `*ptr` *is* `a`: you can read it and you can assign to it.

Reading through a pointer (the notebook's `ptr1.c`):

blocks.caption: ptr1.c

blocks.text: Writing through a pointer (`ptr2.c`). The variable `a` changes even though the assignment never names `a`:

blocks.caption: ptr2.c

blocks.text:
Memory before and after `*ptr = -33;` (pretend addresses):

| address | name | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | `a` | 99 | **-33** |
| 1008 | `ptr` | 1000 | 1000 |

`ptr` itself did not change. Only the object it points to did.

### Three jobs for `*`, two for `&`

| You see | Where | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `int *p;` | in a declaration | `p` is a pointer to `int` |
| `*p` | in front of a pointer, in an expression | the object `p` points to |
| `a * b` | between two values | multiplication |
| `&a` | in front of an object | the address of `a` |
| `a && b` | between two conditions | logical AND |

So `*p * *q` means "the int `p` points to, times the int `q` points to". And `*&a` is just `a`: take the address of `a`, then follow it back.

### `p = q` versus `*p = *q`

This is the difference that exam traces test.

- `p = q;` copies the **address**. Now `p` points wherever `q` points. No `int` changes.
- `*p = *q;` copies the **value**. The object `p` points at gets the value of the object `q` points at. No pointer changes.

Here is a trace. Follow it with the tables underneath.

blocks.caption: trace.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o trace trace.c
$ ./trace
1: 10 20
2: 20 20
3: x = 10, y = 7
4: x = 8, y = 7

blocks.text:
Memory after each step (`x` at 1000, `y` at 1004):

| after line | `x` | `y` | `p` | `q` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `int *q = &y;` | 10 | 20 | 1000 (→x) | 1004 (→y) |
| `p = q;` | 10 | 20 | 1004 (→y) | 1004 (→y) |
| `*p = 7;` | 10 | **7** | 1004 (→y) | 1004 (→y) |
| `q = &x;` | 10 | 7 | 1004 (→y) | 1000 (→x) |
| `*q = *p + 1;` | **8** | 7 | 1004 (→y) | 1000 (→x) |

Method for any trace: keep one column per variable. For a pointer, write which object it points to. When you see `*p`, look up where `p` points and use (or change) **that** column.

blocks.q: In trace.c, suppose line `p = q;` were `*p = *q;` instead. What would lines 2 and 3 print?
blocks.a: `*p = *q` copies 20 into `x` and `p` still points at `x`. Line 2 prints `2: 20 20`. Then `*p = 7` changes `x`, so line 3 prints `3: x = 7, y = 20`.

blocks.text:
### `NULL`: a pointer to nothing

The name `NULL`, from the header `<stddef.h>` (also available through `<stdio.h>`), means "no object". A pointer that holds `NULL` is a **null pointer**.

```c
#include <stddef.h>

int *ptr = NULL;
```

The literal `0` also works, but `NULL` says what you mean. The **only safe thing** to do with a null pointer is to test it:

| Test that `ptr` is null | Test that `ptr` is not null |
|---|---|
| `if (ptr == NULL)` | `if (ptr != NULL)` |
| `if (!ptr)` | `if (ptr)` |

A null pointer works like a signal: "there is no object here". It can mark the end of a list of pointers (much like `'\0'` ends a string) or report an error. Later in the course, library functions such as `malloc` and `fopen` return `NULL` when they fail.

blocks.caption: nulltest.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o nulltest nulltest.c
$ ./nulltest
ptr is NULL: do not use *ptr
*ptr = 5

blocks.text:
### Dereferencing `NULL` is undefined behaviour

`*ptr` when `ptr` is `NULL` asks for "the object at no object". The C standard calls this **undefined behaviour**: anything may happen. On our Linux machines the program is usually killed with a *segmentation fault* (an access to memory the program may not touch), but you must not rely on that.

blocks.caption: ptr3.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o ptr3 ptr3.c
$ ./ptr3
Segmentation fault
$ echo $?
139
blocks.caption: gcc gives no warning here. On one run on Ubuntu the shell reported the crash (some shells add "(core dumped)"); 139 = 128 + 11, signal 11 is the segmentation fault. The notebook shows the same crash as "exited with code -11".

blocks.text: An **uninitialized** pointer is worse than `NULL`: it holds a leftover value that may look like a real address. `int *ptr; *ptr = 5;` is undefined behaviour. With `-Wall` gcc usually warns: `warning: 'ptr' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]`. Habit: give every pointer a value when you declare it, either the address of an object or `NULL`.

Match the types. `double d = 2.5; int *p = &d;` gives `warning: initialization of 'int *' from incompatible pointer type 'double *'`. Reading `*p` would treat the bytes of a `double` as an `int`. Use `double *p = &d;`.

### Key points

- `*p` is the object `p` points to: `x = *p;` reads it, `*p = 5;` writes it.
- `p = q;` copies an address (now they point at the same object). `*p = *q;` copies a value (no pointer moves).
- In a trace, keep one column per variable and record where each pointer points.
- `NULL` (from `<stddef.h>`) means no object. Only test it: `p == NULL`, `!p`, `p != NULL`, `p`.
- Dereferencing a null or uninitialized pointer is undefined behaviour (often "Segmentation fault"). Initialize every pointer.

topics.title: Pointer parameters: changing the caller's variables
topics.examNote: Writing a function that changes its caller's variables through pointers (`swap`, putting values in order, rotating) is a standard handwritten-code task. Marks go for the `T *` parameters, `*` on every use inside, and `&` at the call.

blocks.text:
### Why `badswap` fails

On Day 2 you learned that C passes arguments **by value**: each parameter is a new variable that gets a **copy** of the argument. The notebook's first attempt at `swap` shows the problem:

blocks.caption: badswap.c (c/src/pointers)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o badswap badswap.c
$ ./badswap
before calling swap: a = 1.500000, b = 99.900000
inside swap: x = 99.900000, y = 1.500000
after calling swap: a = 1.500000, b = 99.900000

blocks.text:
`swap` did swap something: its own copies. A memory picture while `swap` is running:

```
 main's variables            swap's variables
 +--------+------+           +--------+-----------------+
 | a 1000 | 1.5  |  copied   | x 2000 | 1.5  -> 99.9    |
 | b 1008 | 99.9 |  ------>  | y 2008 | 99.9 -> 1.5     |
 +--------+------+           | tmp    | 1.5             |
                             +--------+-----------------+
```

`x` and `y` are different objects at different addresses. When `swap` returns, `x`, `y` and `tmp` disappear, and `a` and `b` were never touched. The values of the parameters are **not** copied back.

### The fix: pass the addresses

For `swap` to change `a` and `b`, it needs to know **where** they are. So the caller passes `&a` and `&b`, and the parameters become pointers (`swap.c`):

blocks.caption: swap.c (c/src/pointers)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o swap swap.c
$ ./swap
before calling swap: a = 1.500000, b = 99.900000
inside swap: x = 99.900000, y = 1.500000
after calling swap: a = 99.900000, b = 1.500000

blocks.text:
Now the picture at the start of the call is:

```
 main's variables                swap's variables
 +--------+------+              +--------+------+
 | a 1000 | 1.5  | <----------- | x      | 1000 |
 | b 1008 | 99.9 | <----------- | y      | 1008 |
 +--------+------+              | tmp    |  ?   |
                                +--------+------+
```

The three lines of `swap`, step by step:

| statement | meaning | `a` | `b` | `tmp` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (start) | | 1.5 | 99.9 | ? |
| `double tmp = *x;` | tmp = the object at 1000 | 1.5 | 99.9 | 1.5 |
| `*x = *y;` | object at 1000 = object at 1008 | **99.9** | 99.9 | 1.5 |
| `*y = tmp;` | object at 1008 = tmp | 99.9 | **1.5** | 1.5 |

Note that `tmp` is a plain `double`, not a pointer: it holds a value.

blocks.q: C still passes by value. How can swap change a and b now?
blocks.a: `x` gets a **copy** of the address 1000. But a copy of an address leads to the same house: `*x` is `main`'s `a`. Changing `x` itself (say `x = y;`) would still change nothing in `main`. Changing `*x` changes `a`.

blocks.text:
### The recipe

To let a function change a caller's variable of type `T`:

1. Make the parameter a pointer: `T *p`.
2. Inside the function, write `*p` every time you mean the caller's variable.
3. Call it with the address: `f(&var)`.

| function header | call | can it change `n` in the caller? |
|---|---|---|
| `void inc(int n)` | `inc(n)` | no (changes a copy) |
| `void inc(int *n)` | `inc(&n)` | yes, with `*n = *n + 1;` |

This also explains Day 5: an array argument decays to a pointer to its first element, which is why a function could change the caller's array.

Mismatched calls. With `void swap(double *x, double *y)`, the call `swap(a, b)` is a compile **error**:

```
e1.c:12:10: error: incompatible type for argument 1 of 'swap'
e1.c:3:19: note: expected 'double *' but argument is of type 'double'
```

The other way round, writing `x = y;` instead of `*x = *y;` inside `swap` compiles but only moves the local pointers: the caller sees no change.

To add 1 to the int `p` points to, write `*p = *p + 1;` or `(*p)++;`. Do **not** write `*p++;`: the `++` applies to the pointer `p` itself and moves it (pointer arithmetic, Day 12), and gcc -Wall warns that the value is not used.

blocks.q: Write the header and body of a function `inc` that adds one to its caller's `int`, and the call that adds one to `int count = 0;`.
blocks.a: `void inc(int *n) { *n = *n + 1; }` and the call `inc(&count);`. After the call `count` is 1.

blocks.text: Copy c/src/pointers/badswap.c and swap.c into a folder, compile both with gcc -std=c17 -Wall, and run them. Then change swap.c so main calls swap(a, b) without the & and read gcc's error. Then put the & back and change *x = *y; to x = y; to see that it compiles but no longer swaps.

### Key points

- C passes arguments by value: a function gets copies and cannot change the caller's variables through them.
- To change a caller's variable, pass its address (`&a`) to a pointer parameter (`T *x`) and use `*x` inside.
- `swap`: `T tmp = *x; *x = *y; *y = tmp;` with `tmp` a plain `T`.
- The pointer itself is still a copy: assigning to `x` changes nothing for the caller; assigning to `*x` does.
- Add one through a pointer with `*p = *p + 1;` or `(*p)++`, never `*p++`.

flashcards.back: A value that is the address of an object. A pointer variable stores one; `T *p` can hold the address of a `T`.
The address of the object `x`. Its type is `T *` when `x` has type `T`.

flashcards.front: Declare `p` as a pointer to `double` and make it point at `double d`.

flashcards.back: `p` is a pointer to `int`; `q` is a plain `int`. For two pointers write `int *p, *q;`.

flashcards.front: How do you print a pointer `p` with printf?
flashcards.back: `printf("%p\n", (void *) p);` It prints a hexadecimal address that changes from run to run.

flashcards.front: How many bytes is a pointer on our 64-bit Linux machines?
What does `*p` mean in an expression?
flashcards.back: Dereference: the object `p` points to. `x = *p;` reads it, `*p = 5;` writes it.
`p = q;` copies the address, so both point at the same object. `*p = *q;` copies the value from `q`'s object into `p`'s object.
Just `a`: the address of `a`, followed back.

flashcards.front: What is `NULL` and which header defines it?
flashcards.back: A pointer value meaning "no object", from `<stddef.h>`. A pointer holding it is a null pointer.

flashcards.front: What can you safely do with a null pointer?
flashcards.back: Only test it: `p == NULL`, `!p`, `p != NULL`, `if (p)`. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.

flashcards.front: What happens if you dereference `NULL` or an uninitialized pointer?
flashcards.back: Undefined behaviour. On Linux it often crashes with "Segmentation fault" (exit status 139), but nothing is guaranteed.

flashcards.front: Why can't `void swap(double x, double y)` swap the caller's variables?
flashcards.back: Pass by value: `x` and `y` are copies. Swapping them does nothing to the caller's `a` and `b`, and the copies vanish on return.
`void swap(int *x, int *y) { int tmp = *x; *x = *y; *y = tmp; }` called as `swap(&a, &b);`

flashcards.front: Three steps to let a function change a caller's `T` variable
Inside `void f(int *p)`, what is the difference between `p = &local;` and `*p = 9;`?
flashcards.back: `p = &local;` only changes `f`'s copy of the pointer: the caller sees nothing. `*p = 9;` changes the caller's int.

quiz.explain: Start: p→b, q→c, r→b, so A is `8 15 8`. `q = p` makes q→b; `p = &a` makes p→a: B is `4 8 8`. `*q = *p * 2` sets b = 8; `*r = *r + 1` sets b = 9 (r also points at b); `*p = 0` sets a = 0. C is `0 9 9`, D is `0 9 15` (nothing pointed at c after `q = p`). Same style as 2016F Q3.
`prod = 3 * 5 = 15`. `*q = *q - *p` sets n = 2. `p = q` makes p point at n, so `*p = *p * 10` sets n = 20. m is never changed.
`a` is a copy of x, so x stays 1. `b` holds the address of y, so each call adds 1 to y: 1 → 2 → 3.
`p` is a copy of the address of x. `p = &local;` changes only that copy, so `*p = 9` writes into `local`, not x. (Note: pointing at `local` is fine here because it is used before g returns.)
After `swap(&a, &b)`: a = 2, b = 1, c = 3. After `swap(&b, &c)`: b = 3, c = 1.
`p` and `&v` are the same address, so both calls halve v: 9 → 4.5 → 2.25. `%.2f` prints two decimals.

`!p` is true when p is NULL, so `one` prints. Then p points at k, so `if (p)` is true: `two`. `*p` is k, which is 0 (false), so `three` is not printed. Note the difference: `if (p)` tests the pointer, `if (*p)` tests the int.

quiz.q: After `int *p, q;`, what are the types of `p` and `q`?
quiz.explain: The `*` belongs to the name next to it. Write `int *p, *q;` for two pointers.

quiz.q: Given `void swap(double *x, double *y)` and `double a = 1, b = 2;`, which call swaps `a` and `b`?
quiz.explain: The parameters need addresses of doubles: `&a` and `&b`. `swap(a, b)` is a compile error (incompatible type for argument), and `*a` is an error because `a` is not a pointer.

quiz.q: Pretend addresses: `int x = 6;` is at 1000 and `int *p = &x;` is at 1008. Give the values of `x`, `&x`, `p`, `*p` and `&p`.
quiz.explain: `p` holds the address of `x`. `*p` follows it to `x`. `&p` is where the pointer itself lives.

quiz.q: Explain in one or two sentences why the notebook's `badswap` prints swapped values inside the function but not after it returns.
quiz.answer: C passes arguments by value: `x` and `y` are copies of `a` and `b`, so swapping them does not change `a` and `b`, and the copies disappear when `swap` returns.
quiz.explain: The fix is to pass `&a` and `&b` to `double *` parameters and swap `*x` and `*y`.

quiz.q: What is wrong with `int *p; *p = 3;` and how do you fix it?
quiz.answer: `p` is uninitialized, so it does not point at a valid `int`; writing `*p` is undefined behaviour. Make it point at an object first: `int n; int *p = &n; *p = 3;`.
quiz.explain: gcc -Wall usually warns "'p' is used uninitialized". Giving a pointer `NULL` does not help either: dereferencing NULL is also undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: Given `int n = 4; int *p;`, write one statement that makes `p` point at `n`, then one statement that sets `n` to 0 without naming `n`.
quiz.explain: Not `*p = &n;` (that stores an address into an int) and not `p = 0;` (that makes p a null pointer).

write.prompt: Write a function `minfirst` that gets pointers to two `int` variables and rearranges them so that the first holds the smaller value and the second the larger. Write a `main` that calls it on `a = 9`, `b = 4` and prints both, twice.
write.explain:
The caller's variables must change, so the parameters are `int *x, int *y` and `main` passes `&a, &b`. Inside, every use of the caller's values is `*x` or `*y`. The swap only happens when they are out of order; `tmp` is a plain `int`. The second call finds them already in order and changes nothing.

```
$ ./minfirst
a = 4, b = 9
a = 4, b = 9
```

rubric.item: three-step swap through `*x` and `*y` with an `int tmp`

pitfalls: Comparing `x > y` compares addresses, not values.
Calling `minfirst(a, b)`: compile error, the function needs addresses.

write.prompt: Complete `swap` so it exchanges the values of two `int` variables in its caller, and complete the call. The program must print `a = -2, b = 5`.
pitfalls: `int tmp = x;` stores an address in an int (gcc warns).
Writing `x = y;` swaps only the local pointers.

write.prompt: Write a function `rotate` that gets pointers to three `int` variables and moves each value one place to the right, with the last value moving to the front: if the caller has `x = 1, y = 2, z = 3`, after `rotate(&x, &y, &z)` they are `x = 3, y = 1, z = 2`. Use no arrays. Write a `main` that rotates `1 2 3` twice, printing the three values after each call.

rubric.item: saves one value in a plain `int tmp` before it is overwritten
assignments in a safe order through `*a`, `*b`, `*c` (e.g. `*c = *b; *b = *a; *a = tmp;`)

pitfalls: Overwriting a value before saving it (e.g. `*b = *a;` first, then `*c = *b;` copies a's value twice).
Forgetting the `*`: `a = b;` only moves the local pointers.
